2.a.Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (TNCDW)

The Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (TNCDW) was established in 1983 by the Government of Tamil Nadu with the Primary objective of social and economic empowerment of women through education, employment, economic development and self-reliance.

The Self-Help Group (SHG) movement in Tamil Nadu was nurtured by TNCDW for the overall development of rural women by instilling a sense of bonding and confidence through a wide range of capacity building activities and forming Cammunity Based Organizations (CBOs) like the Panchayat Level Federations (PLFs), Block Level Federations (BLFs), etc. and facilitating bank credit for income generation through economic activities and various poverty alleviation programmes.

A total of 3.95 lakhs SHGs are active in rural and urban areas of Tamil Nadu. In addition to this, SHGs are also formed and Supported by various Government and Non-Government Organisations (NGOs),

2.b. Self Help Group (SHG) Movement

The seeds of the Self Help Group (SHG) concept for the Socio-economic empowerment of women was sown in 1989 at Dharmapuri. The SHG concept gained momentum under International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) assisted project and with the introduction of the Mahalir Thittam in 1996, it was slowly extended to other districts and by the year 2000, all districts including Chennai

13

District was included under the scheme. Due to the strong SHG base created in the State, the Swarnaajayanthi Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) a Centrally Sponsored Scheme launched in 1999 to address rural poverty with focus on SHG was effectively implemented for economic improvement of the rural poor. During the year 2022-2023, 4,39,349 SHGs have been assisted with a credit linkage of Rs.25,022.19 crore with an average loan size per SHG is Rs.5.68 lakh.

2.c. Poverty Alleviation and Livelihood Missions

The Government of Tamil Nadu is a model welfare State which focuses on inclusive socio-economic development through multivarious schemes that provide opportunities for disadvantaged people to access the benefits of programmes and projects and improve their quality of life. The Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department is vested with the important mandate of poverty alleviation and socio-economic empowerment of the poor, marginalized and vulnerable families through livelihood promotion programmes anchored by the Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women and the World Bank assisted “Yaazhndhu Kaattuvom” Project now continued as Tamil Nadu Rural Transformation Project.

2.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors

In Tamil Nadu, majority of economically productive women are engaged as agricultural labourers. Despite their large presence and contribution to rural economy, their work is limited to less skilled jobs such as sowing, transplanting, weeding, harvesting etc. Further, Women cultivators are very less in number and do not have proper access to inputs (seed, fertilizer), credit facility, organised markets, advanced technologies such as use of drudgery reduction technologies etc. The State shall therefore take necessary measures to support women in agriculture.

Town Panchayats are taking various efforts

to provide protected water supply to all

construction of overhead tanks for sufficient

In all Town Panchayats, water is supplied to the public at the rate of 70 litre per capita per day (LPCD), while in Town Panchayats with Under Ground Sewerage Systems (UGSS), action is being taken to provide water supply at the rate of 135 liters per person per day. Out of the total 487 Town Panchayats, 325 are supplied with drinking water through the Combined Water Supply Schemes maintained by TWAD Board. The remaining Town Panchayats provide water supply through local sources. Currently, 42% of households have their household water connections. The goal is to provide functional household tap connections to all households, ensuring universal access to drinking water.

Key activities of Town Panchayats include augmenting and maintaining water sources, restoring ponds and wells, reusing of recycled treated water and also establishment of new rainwater harvesting arrangements and restoration of existing rain water harvesting structures etc., in all types of buildings through

246

community contributions are important for achieving sustainable water economics.

Major water-related reforms envisaged in Town Panchayats include accessing 20% of water requirements from treated and recycled water, reduction of non revenue water below 20% and restoring water bodies.

Additionally, 21 water supply improvement projects at a total estimated cost of Rs.132.80 crore are being taken up under Kalaignar Nagarpura Mempattu Thittam for the year 2024-25. Once these projects are completed, the number of household connections in Town Panchayats will increase significantly.

13. JALLIKATTU - THE TRADITIONAL AND CULTURAL IDENTITY OF TAMIL NADU

Jallikattu is a traditional event of the rural

people of Tamil Nadu particularly in southern part

of the State. It has a 5,000-year-old tradition and

a history associated with the socio-cultural ethos

of Tamil Nadu. It represents the bond between

the humans and the animals, the bravery of tamil

youth and the agrarian way of tamil life. The bulls

used for the event are the native breeds of the

area; thereby the event also ensures that the

native breeds are preserved. The event is the

testimony to the harmony of Tamil culture as it is

celebrated by Tamil people irrespective of religion

or caste or creed.

The event is mainly associated with the

annual Pongal festival and celebrations with

specific reference to Mattu Pongal day. Besides,

the Mattu Pongal festival, Jallikattu along with its

other variants namely Manjuvirattu / Vadamadu /

95

Erudu Vidum Vizha are conducted during the

pongal festivals of the local temple in the villages

as per the tradition of the respective villages.

Because of incidents of injury and death

associated with the sport - both to the

participants and to the animals. Animal Rights

Organizations called for a ban on the sport,

resulting in the Hon’ble Supreme Court of

India banning the conduct of the event several

times over the past years. However, with protests

from the people of the State against the ban, a

new ordinance was enacted by the State in 2017

to continue the sport, which received the assent

of the President of India to become an Act of

Tamil Nadu Legislature namely, the Jallikattu Act

This included establishment of ornamental fish park for linking all the ornamental hubs for providing good quality seed, feed, training, technology, medicines and to buy back the grown ornamental fish for export.

NFDB approved the proposal and accorded sanction (May 2014) for an amount of ` 2.13 crore. The first instalment of ` 1.06 crore was released (May 2014) and the guidelines of NFDB envisaged submission of UC on physical completion of units by the beneficiaries to the DoF for release of second instalment. The Department identified 237 beneficiaries in 10 districts and released first instalment of subsidy of ` 59.25 lakh during February to June 2015. The Department incurred ` 5.41 lakh for training of beneficiaries in 10 districts. The progress of completion of works of units, for which subsidy had been released, was awaited (September 2015).

The Department had not initiated establishment of ornamental fish retail outlets and transportation vehicles despite sanction and release of funds by NFDB. Thus, failure to establish ornamental fish park, delay in completion of fish hubs and units, impacted the achievement of the envisaged objective.

Similarly, establishment of integrated ornamental fish culture centre at Government Seed Farm, Mettur dam sanctioned (January 2013) under NFDB for ` 13.50 lakh could not be commenced (May 2015), due to delay in handing over of the site by DoF, even after expiry of more than two years from the date of release of first instalment (March 2013) of ` 6.75 lakh.
